title: Mental Health Act revamp urged
article: A provincial court judge is recommending a review of the Mental Health Act following the death of Tamer Roha, who died in police custody of cocaine-induced excited delirium after days of binging on the drug.
Judge Anne Brown released her eight-page report Wednesday on the circumstances surrounding the 27-year-old's death, after hearing six days of testimony at a fatality inquiry into the 2002 incident.
"It is recommended that the Mental Health Act criteria for detention be scheduled for legislative review within the next year," she wrote.
"With particular attention to be paid to the treatment of patients with drug-induced disorders."
Roha was a cocaine abuser and had been in several hospitals and rehabilitation programs for his addiction.

On the day he died, Roha was staying at the Quality Inn in northwest Calgary, where he started behaving in a bizarre manner, screaming incoherently and repeatedly opening and closing his motel room door.
A frantic Roha reportedly then started yelling out "911," and hotel employees called for help.
Once police arrived, they attempted to restrain Roha while waiting for an ambulance crew.
Police moved Roha from the floor to a kneeling position. Shortly thereafter, his body went limp. He was pronounced dead less than an hour later.
The report into the Roha incident details nine recommendations for preventing similar deaths in the future, seven of which are directed at the Calgary Police Service.
Brown suggests a video depicting a person suffering from excited delirium be shown in every subject control training session, something police say is already done.
She also wrote that leaving the victim to their own devices, rather than restraining them, may be an option if medical crews are en route.
As well, a recommendation to the Calgary Health Region suggests "referral information for addicts and their families be broadened and improved."
